newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines strike could hurt Miami.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines strike could hurt Miami.

text.p: A threatened strike by pilots of AMR Corp's American Airlines could throw cargo traffic and travel in Miami into a tailspin and put a damper on the local economy, industry executives said.
"It would be a national disaster," said Robert C. Booth, president of Aviation Management Services, a Miami consulting firm. "There is not enough capacity to make up the difference."
"It would be horrible," said Chris Cook, a Miami-based international marketing executive.
The pilots and carrier must reach a contract agreement by 0001 EST/0501 GMT Feb 15, the end of a legally mandated "cooling off" period, or the pilots could go on strike.
"It would have a significant impact," said Peter Reaveley, head of Miami International Airport's (MIA) route development.
American carries more cargo through Miami International, considered the financial capital of Latin America, than any other airline. In the first nine months of last year, it hauled 148,935 tons.
A study sponsored by American Airlines recently showed it accounts for about 114,000 jobs in Dade County, nearly 10 percent of the area's employment.
"We are very concerned about the impact of a work stoppage," American spokesman Johan Hotard said. "We are concerned about our employees, passengers and the areas we serve."
Reaveley said there would probably be enough alternative capacity for much of the international cargo to continue to fly, but freight forwarders would have to scramble to re-book.
American also carries the most passengers -- about half MIA's total -- with 196 daily departures, according to statistics provided by American and Metro-Dade Aviation Department.
From MIA, American flies to 87 destinations including 44 international locations. That amounts to about 15 million passengers a year, or more than 41,000 passengers a day.
"It is already difficult to book flights. If American went on strike it would be impossible," said Cook, who flies to Latin America at least three times a month.

Not only would freight and travelers to and fro Miami be scrambling for new transportation, but travelers trying to fly within Latin America often fly to American's Miami hub and then to South America.
Despite the dire predictions, MIA's Reaveley said passengers will make other arrangements. "People don't stop flying because an airline is on strike," he said.
Many aviation sources said they believed the dispute would be settled at the last moment or the federal government would intervene.
"There are all sorts of other implications besides the travel and cargo problem. There are huge orders for new planes from Boeing that would be affected," Booth said.
